[< Gr. tpeic (rpt-), three, + chlorin) + acetic.] Used only in the following phrase.—Trichloracetic acid, acetic acid in which the three hydrogen atoms of the methyl radical are replaced by chlorin. The formula of acetic acid being CH3.CO gH, that of trichloroacetic acid is CClg.COoH. Trichloracetic acid is a crystalline solid, easily decomposed.

trichoblast.c: trichoblast (trik’6-blast), n. [< Gr. Opi (cpiy-), hair, + Bdaordc, germ.] In bot., an internal hair, as one of those which project into the intercellular spaces of certain water-plants. See but under mangrove.

trichobranchia.c: trichobranchia (trik-d-brang’ki-i), n.; pl. trich- obranchie (-6). [NI., «Gr. @pt& (tpty-), hair, + Bpdyxia, gills.] A filamentous gill characteristic of most long-tailed ten-footed crustaceans, consisting of a stem beset with many cylindrical filaments, as distinguished from the lamellar gills, or phyllobranchia, of many other crusta- means. The developed arthrobranchia, pleurobranchia, and podobranchize of crawfishes are all of the trichobran- chial type. The whole of the Macrurous Podophthalmia, excepting the genera Gebia and Callianassa, the Prawns, the Shrimps, and the Myside, have trichobranchia. Hualey, Proc. Zool. Soc., 1878, p. 777.
trichobranchia (trik-6-brang’ki-al), a. [< trichobranchia + -al.] Thready or filamentous, as gills; of or pertaining to trichobranchia: as, a trichobranchia gill.

trichobranchiata.c: Trichobranchiata (trik-d-brang-ki-a’t&), n. pl. [NL.: see trichobranchia.] Those macrurous crustaceans which have trichobranchia.

trichobranchiate.c: trichobranchiate (trik-6-brang’ki-at), a. [< trichobranchia + -ate.] Having trichobranchia, as a crawfish. [< Gr. Opié (Tptx-), a hair, + xapréc, fruit.] In bot., having hairy fruit; hairy-fruited.

trichocarpous.c: trichocarpous (trik-0-kir’pus), a. is in? er Trichocephalus axis, forms within the scleroblast a sheaf of exceedingly fine fibrillee which may be straight or twisted; also, one of these fibrille: as, “fine fibrille or trichites,” Sollas.—2. In lithol., one of various dark-colored (or even black) opaque microlith, having more or less of a curved and twisted form: frequently seen in thin sections of vitreous rocks, especially in obsidian. II, a. Same as trichitic. Trichite sheaves form in some sponges... a dense accumulation within the cortex. Hnecyc. Brit., XXII. 418.

trichocephalide.c: Trichocephalide (trik’6-se-fal’/i-dé), n. pl. [NL., < Trichocephalus + -ide.] A family of nematoid worms, typified by the genus Trichocephalus.

trichocephalus.c: Trichocephalus (trik-9-sef’a-lus), n. [NL. (Goeze, 1782), < Gr. Opt (rpt-), a hair, + xe- gary, head.] 1. A genus of nematoid worms, typical of the family Trichocephalide. The best-known species is 7. dispar, found sometimes in the human intestine, 1 to 2 inches long, with the -head and anterior Vege of the body filamentous. 7’. finis is the cecum-worm of sheep. Trichocephalus 2. [l. c.] The detached hectocotylized third left arm of the male argonaut, deposited in the pallial cavity of the female, and regarded as a parasite by Delle Chiaje, who called it Trichocephalus acetabularia, making the word a pseudogeneric name. See cut under Argonautide.

trichocladose.c: trichocladose (tri-kok’la-dos), a. [< Gr. rpiya, in three (< rpeic (tpi-), three), + «Addoc, branch.] Trifid or trichotomous, as the clad or branches of acladome. See trine. Sollas.

trichocladus.c: Trichocladus(tri-kok’la-dus),n. [NL. (Persoon, 1807), so called with ref. to the woolly branches, € Gr. Opig (tpix-), hair, + KAddoc, branch.] 1, A genus of polypetalous shrubs, of the order Hamamelidex, distinguished from the type genus Hamamelis by mucronate anthers, and flowers with the parts in fives. The 2 species are natives of South Africa, They are evergreen shrubs with opposite or alternate entire leaves, and white flowers densely aggregated into small terminal heads, bearing long narrow petals with revolute margins, the pistillate flowers apetalous. 1. ellipticus is remarkable for the reddish wool clothing the under surface of the leaves; and 7’. crinites, the hairbranch-tree, for its branchlets and petioles, which are hirsute with blackish hairs. a [l. ¢.] In zool., a trichocladose sponge-spic- e.

trichoclasia.c: trichoclasia (trik-6-kla’si-’), n. [< Gr. pig (tptx-), hair, + kdaovc, a fracture.] A brittle condition of the hair. Also trichoclasis.

trichocryptosis.c: trichocryptosis (trik’6-krip-td’sis), n. [NL., < Gr. pig (rpt-), hair, + xpurréc, hidden, + -osis.] Inflammation of the hair-follicles.

trichocyst.c: trichocyst (trik’6-sist), ». [< Gr. Opié (pry-), hair, + toric, bladder: see cyst.] A hair-cell; one of the minute rodlike or hairlike bodies developed in the subcuticular layer of many in- fusorians: so named by G. J. Allman in 1855. They represent or resemble the chide or thread-cells of ecelenterates.

trichocystic.c: trichocystic (trik-6-sis’tik), a. [< trichocyst + -ic.| Pertaining to or having the character of trichocyst: as, a trichocystic formation.

trichoda.c: Trichoda (tri-ko’dii), n. [NL., < Gr. tpiyedye, contr. of rpzyoetdye, like a hair, < Opi (racy-), hair, + eidoc,form.] A genus of ciliate infusorian, established by O. F, Miiller in 1786, giving name to the former family Trichodide (or Trichodina). Many animalcules have been referred to this genus which are now excluded from it. It is now placed in the family Ophryoglenidz, and retained for such species as 7. car- nium, found in putrid infusions, and 7’. pirum, of pond- water. These closely resemble forms of Enchelys, but have a minute vibratile membrane inclosed in the oral fossa. They are freeswimming, elastic, but of somewhat persistent ovate or pyriform figure, with the mouth at the obliquely truncated anterior end, approached by an oval peristome; the general cuticular surface is finely ciliated throughout, and a circlet of longer cilia surrounds the oral fossa.

trichodectes.c: Trichodectes (trik-6-dek’téz), mn. [NL (Nitzsch),< Gr. Opié (prey-), hair, + déxryc, taker, < dékeobat, déyecba, receive, take.] A genus of mallophagous insects. 1. spherocephalus is the redheaded sheep-louse, found in the wool of sheep in Europe and America. See sheep-louse, 2.

trichodon.c: Trichodon (trik’6-don), n. [NL. (Cuvier, 1829, after Steller), < Gr. @if (cpiy-), hair, + ddovc (adopt-) = K. tooth.] The typical genus of the family Trichodontide. T. stelleri, the sandfish, is found in Alaska and south to California. See but under sandfish. -Trichodontide (trik-d-don’ti-dé), n.pl. [NL., < Prichodon(t-) + -ide.| A family of acanthopterygian fishes, typified by the genus Tyi- codon; the sandfishes.

trichodontoid.c: trichodontoid (trik-6-don’toid), n. and a. I, n. A fish of the family Trichodontide. II. a. Of, or having characters of, the Tricho- dontide.

trichogen.c: trichogen (trik’6-jen), ». [< Gr. Opié (rTpLx-), hair, + -yevgc, producing: see -gen.] A substance or preparation used for promoting the growth of the hair.

trichogenous.c: trichogenous (tri-koj’e-nus), a. [As trichogen + -ous.] Encouraging the growth of hair.

trichoglosside.c: Trichoglosside (trik-0-glos’i-dé), v. pl. [NL., < Trichoglossus + -ide.] The Trichoglossine ranked as a family.

trichoglossine.c: Trichoglossine (trik’6-glo-si’né),”. pl. [NL., < Trichoglossus + -ine.] A subfamily of Psit- tacite, typified by the genus Trichoglossus, and inexactly synonymous with Loriine, or inelud- ing the latter; the brush-tongued parrakeets, among the small parrots called lories and lorikeets. With the exception of the genus Coryllis or Lo- riculus (usually put here, but probably belonging elsewhere), these parrakeets have the tongue brushy, beset with papille or filaments, and used for licking the nectar of flowers and the soft pulp of fruits. There are more than 80 species, characteristic of the Australian regions and Polynesia, but also extending into the Malay countries. They are among the smaller parrots, and of chiefly green 6469 or red colors. One set of species has a short broad tail; these are the broad-tailed lories, as of the genera Domicella and Coriphilus (see cut under domicella); but the most characteristic representatives are wedgetailed.
trichoglossine (trik-d-glos’in), a. Of or pertaining to the Trichoglossine.

trichoglossus.c: Trichoglossus (trik-0-glos’us),. [NL. (Vigors and Horsfield, 1826), < Gr. @pié (pry-), hair, + yAdooa, tongue.] Theleading genus of Trichoglossine, used with varying limits; the lories most properly so called. All are brush-tongued and wedgetailed; they are of moderate or small size, and Swainson’s Lory (7rzchoglossus nove-hollandiz). chiefly green and red. The genus in a usual acceptation contains about 40 species, or half of the Trichoglossine. Swainson’s lory of Australia is a characteristic example, usent. green, beautifully varied with red, blue, and yet- Ow.

trichogramma.c: Trichogramma (trik-0-gram’i),n. [NL. (West- wood, 1833), < @if (rpt-),. hair, + ypaypa, a writing.}] A curious genus of hymenopterous S Be: t), Trichogramma miniuta. @, fly with wings folded; 4, front wing; c, hind wing; d, leg; e,antenna. (All enlarged.) parasites, of the family Chalcididz, and typical of the subfamily Trichogrammine. One rare species is known in Europe, but several are found in North America, where the individuals are extremely abundant, as of 7. minute. They are all parasitic in the eggs of lepidopterous insects and of sawflies.

trichogrammine.c: Trichogrammine (trik’6-gra-mi’né), n. pl. [NL. (l. O. Howard, 1885), < Trichogramma + -ine.| A subfamily of parasitic hymenopters, of the family Chalcididz, containing the smallest species of the family, characterized by their three-pointed tarsi (thus forming the section Trimera) and the regular fringe of minute bristles on the wings. They vary in color from bright yellow to reddish brown, and are all parasitic in the eggs of other insects. Also Trichogrammatoide (Forster, 1856). See cut under Trichogramma. (NL., < Gr. Opié

trichogyne.c: trichogyne (trik’0-jin), n. (rpt-), hair, + yur7,afemale.] In bot., a long thin hairlike sae springing from the tricho- phorie part of the procarp of certain crypto- gams, and serving as a receptive organ of reproduction. See procarp, Floridez.

trichogynic.c: trichogynic (trik-6-jin’ik), a [« trichogyne + -ic.] In bot., of or pertaining to the trichogyne.

trichologia.c: trichologia (trik-6-10’ji-4), n. [NL., < Gr. as if *rpiyodoyia,< Tpryodoyetv, pluck hairs (as a symptom),< Opié (cpiy-), hair, + Aéyewv, gather, pick.] Carphologia.

trichology.c: trichology (tri-kol’6-ji), n. [< Gr. Oot (rpix-), hair, + -Aoyia, < Aéyevv, speak: see -ology.] The science treating of the anatomy, diseases, function, etc., of the hair.

trichoma.c: trichoma (tri-k0’mii), ». [NL., <¢ Gr. tpizoua, a growth of hair, < rpcyovv, furnish or cover with hair, < OpiE (they-), hair.] 1. In pathol., an affection of the hair, otherwise called plica.— 2. In bot., one of the cellular filaments which form the substance of a suborder of algee, the Nosto- chinee. Farlow, Marine Alge, p. 11.

trichomanes.c: Trichomanes (tri-kom’a-néz), n. [NL. (Tourne- fort, 1700), < Gr. tpcyouavéc, a kind of fern (ef. Tptyouavia, a passion for long hair, tpcyouaveiv, have a passion for long hair), <¢ Opié (rpzy-), hair, + paivecba:,be mad. Cf. the E. names bristle-fern Trichonotus and maidenhair.] A large genus of hymenophyllaceous ferns, having the sori marginal, terminating a vein, and more or less sunken in the frond. The sporangia are sessile on the lower part of a cylindrical, filiform, usually elongated receptacle, and Bristle-fern (Trzchomanes radicans). the indusia are tubular or funnelshaped, and entire or two-lipped at the mouth. About 100 species are known, natives of tropical and temperate countries, including two in the southern United States. All are popularly called bristle-ferns. See bristle-fern, and cut (e) under sorus.

trichomaphyte.c: trichomaphyte (tri-kom’a-fit), n. [< Gr. tpixo- pa, a growth of hair (see trichoma), + @vrdv, a plant.] <A eryptogamie growth which was formerly thought to be the cause of trichoma.

trichomatose.c: trichomatose (tri-kom’a-tés),a. [< trichoma(t-) + -ose.] Matted or agglutinated together; affected with trichoma: said of hair.

trichome.c: trichome (tri’kom), ». [< NL. trichoma, q. v.] An outgrowth from the epidermis of plants, as a hair, scale, bristle, or prickle. These may be very various in form and function, but morphologically they have a common origin.

trichomonadide.c: Trichomonadide (trik’6-mo-nad’i-de), n. pl. [NL., < Trichomonas (-monad-) + -idz.] A family of flagellate infusorian, characterized by the tapering form posteriorly, and the development of several flagella and bodies like trichocyst at the anterior extremity.

trichomonas.c: Trichomonas (tri-kom’6-nas),”. [NL. (Ehren- berg, 1838), < Gr. OpiE (tpty-), hair, + povdc, single.] The typical genus of Trichomonadidez. T. melolontha infests the cockchafer. T. vaginalis is found in the secretions of the human vagina.

trichomycosis.c: trichomycosis (trik’6-mi-k6’sis), n. [NL., < Gr. pig (tpty-), hair, + pbxyc, fungus, + -osis.] Same as tineal.

trichomycteride.c: Trichomycteride (trik’6-mik-ter’i-dé), n. pl. [NL., < Trichomycterus + -idz.] A family of fishes: same as Pygidiide.

trichomycterine.c: Trichomycterine (trik-0-mik-te-ri/né),. pl. [NL., < Trichomycterus + -ine.] A subfamily of trichomyeteroid fishes, with the dorsal fin posterior, and behind the ventrals when the latter are present. It includes most species of the family. Also Trichomycterina and Pygidiine.
trichomycterine (trik-6-mik’te-rin), a. and n. I. a. Of, or having characters of, the Tricho- myctering. II. n. A fish of the subfamily Trichomycte- rine.

trichomycteroid.c: trichomycteroid (trik-0-mik’te-roid), a. and n. I. a. Of, or having characters of, the Tricho- mycteride. II. ». A fish of the family Trichomycteride.

trichomycterus.c: Trichomycterus (trik’6-mik-té’rus), ». [NL. (Cuvier and Valenciennes, 1846), < Gr. Opié (rpt-), hair, + wvar7p, nostril.] Same as Pygidium, 2.

trichonotid.c: trichonotid (trik-d-nd’toid), a. and n. I. a. Of or relating to the Trichonotide. II, x. A fish of the family Trichonotide.

trichonotide.c: Trichonotide (trik-d-not’i-dé), n. pl. [NL., < Trichonotus + -ide.) A family of acanthopterygian fishes, represented by the genus Tricho- notus.

trichonotus.c: Trichonotus (trik-6-n0’tus), n. [NL.(Bloch and Schneider, 1801), < Gr. OpiE (racy-), hair, + véroc, back.] 1. In ichth., the typical genus of Tri- chonotidez: so called from the long filamentous anterior dorsal ray of 7. setigerous, the original species. The body is long and subcylindrical, with Trichonotus cycloid scales of moderate size; the eyes look upward; the teeth are in villiform bands on the jaws; the long dorsal fin is spineless; the anal is also long; the ventrals are jugular, with one spine and five rays; and the caudal vertebre are very numerous. 2. In entom., a generic name which has been used for certain beetles and flies, but is in each case preoccupied in ichthyology.

trichopathic.c: trichopathic (trik-0-path’ik), a. [< trichopathy + -ic.| Relating to disease of the hair.

trichopathy.c: trichopathy (tri-kop’a-thi), ». [< Gr. Opié (tpty-), hair, + -arabia, < 7d6oc, suffering.] Treatment of diseases of the hair.

trichophocine.c: Trichophocine (trik’6-f6-si’né),. pl. [NL., < Gr. GoiE (Tpix-), hair, + oxy, a seal, + -ine.] A subfamily of the Otariidz, or eared seals, in- eluding the hair-seals as distinguished from the fur-seals (Ulophocine). There is no type genus.
trichophocine (trik-0-f0’sin), a. Pertaining to the Trichophocine, or having their characters.

trichophore.c: trichophore (trik’0-for), n. [« Gr. Opie (Tpex-), hair, + -@opec, < dépexy = E. bear.] 1. In bot., the special cell or chain of cells in certain al- ge which bears the trichogyne. See Floridee. Bennett and Murray, Cryptog. Bot., p. 199.—2. In zool., a process of the integument of certain annelids, as Polycheta, within which are developed the peculiar chitinous see of the parapodia, and which incloses the bases of the pen- eil-like bundles of sets (whence the name). See cut under pygidium.

trichophoric.c: trichophoric (trik-6-for’ik), a. [< trichophore + -ic.] In bot.: (a) Of or pertaining to the trichophore: as, the trichophoric apparatus. (b) Of the nature of a trichophore: as, the tricho- phorie part of the procarp of certain crypto- gams.

trichophyton.c: Trichophyton (tri-kof’i-ton), ». [NL., < Gr. Ope (Tpry-), hair, + gvrdv, a plant.] A genus .of minute saprolegnious fungi, parasitic on the skin of man, where they grow luxuriantly in and beneath the epidermis, in the hair-follicles, etc. T. tonsurans produces the skin-disease known as tinea or ringworm. See dermatophyte, tineal.

trichoplax.c: Trichoplax (trik’6-plaks), n. [NL., < Gr. @pié (rpt-), hair, + 7Aaé, a plate.] A supposed generic type of animal, of wholly undetermined affinities, so called from the ciliated platelike surface. The species is 7. adherent.

trichopore.c: trichopore (trik’o-spor),. _[< Gr. 6pif (pix-), hair, + oopa, seed: see spore2.] In bot., one of the peculiar spores of the Hyphomycetes: same, or nearly the same, as conidium.

trichopter.c: trichopter (tri-kop’tér),. [< Lrichoptera, q. v.] A member of the Trichoptera; a caddisfly.

trichoptera.c: Trichoptera (tri-kop’te-ri), n. pl. [NL., neut. pl. of trichopterous: see trichopterous.] A subordinal group of neuropterous insects, the caddisflies: so called because the wings are generally hairy to an extent not found in other Newrop- tera. The posterior wings are folded in rest; the mandibles are rudimentary. _ The group is approximately the same as Phryganeida, being composed of the families Phryganeidx, Limnophilide, and sundry others. See cut under caddisworm.;

trichopteran.c: trichopteran (tri-kop’te-ran), a.and n. [< Trichoptera + -an.] I, a. Same as trichopterous. II. x. A member of the Trichoptera; any cad- dis-fly or phryganeid.

trichopterous.c: trichopterous (tri-kop’te-rus), a. [< NL. tri- chopterus, hairy-winged, < Gr. pig (cpiy-), hair, + xrepdv, wing.] Belonging to the Trichoptera.

trichopterygid.c: trichopterygid (trik-op-ter’i-jid), a.and ». I, a. Pertaining to the Trichopterygide; relating to or resembling a trichopterygid. IT. n. A beetle of the family Trichopterygide.

trichopterygide.c: Trichopterygide (tri-kop-te-rij’i-dé), n. pl. [NL. (Burmeister, 1845), < Trichopteryx + -idz.] A family of clavicorn beetles, including the smallest beetles known. The antenne are verticillate with long hairs, and the wings are fringed with hair. A few species are apterous. The larve are active and carnivorous; some of them feed on poduran. Some are myrmecophilous; others live under bark. In the genera Aderces, Astatopteryx, and Neuglenes the phenomenon of alternate generation has been noticed, a blind apterous generation alternating with one in which the individuals have eyes and wings. About 150 species are known, of which about 60 inhabit the United States.

trichopteryx.c: Trichopteryx (tri-kop’te-riks), n. [NL. (Hiib- ner, 1816),< Gr. Opis (rpty-), hair, + rrépvé, wing. 1. A genus of geometrid moths.—2. A genus of clavicorn beetles, typical of the family Tri- chopterygida. Kirby, 1826. They have the antenne elongate, eleven-jointed, the prothorax not constricted behind, the abdomen with six ventral segments, the hind come distant, and the mesosternum carinate. The species are found on dung and vegetable debris. Over 60 species are known, and the genus is represented in Europe, Asia, and North and South America. trichord,. A Middle English form of treacher.

trichord.c: trichord (tri’kérd), n. and a. [< Gr. tpixopdoc, having three strings, < Tpei¢ (rp-), three, + yopdA, 6470 string: see cord}, chord.) I, n. In music, any instrument with three strings, especially the three-stringed lute. II. a. Having three strings; characterized by three strings.—Trichord pianoforte, a pianoforte in which most of the digitals have each three strings tuned in unison.:

trichorexis.c: trichorexis (trik-d-rek’sis), mn. [NL., ¢ Gr. 6pig (tpix-), hair, + pygic, a breaking, ¢ pyyvivat, break.] Brittleness of the hair.—Trichorexis nodose, a disease of the hair characterized by brittleness and the formation of swellings on the shaft. b

trichorrheatrichorrhea.c: trichorrhea, trichorrhea (trik-o-rée’i), n. [NL., < Gr. Opié (Tptyx-), hair, + poia, a flowing, < priv, flow.] Falling of the hair; alopecia.

trichosanthes.c: Trichosanthes (trik-o-san’théz), ». [NL. (Lin- ness, 1737), named from the fringed petals; < Gr. Opie (rpt-), hair, + avOoc, flower.] A genus of plants, of the order Cucurbitacee and tribe Cucumerinex. Itis characterized by entire calyx-lobes, a fiveparted wheel-shaped fringed corolla, conduplicate anther-cells, and numerous polymorphous seeds, There are about 42 species, natives of tropical Asia, northern Australia, and Polynesia, They are annual or perennial climbers, sometimes with a tuberous root, bearing entire or lobed and cordate leaves and unbranched or forking tendrils. The flowers are white and moncecious —the male racemed, the female solitary —and followed by a fleshy smooth or furrowed fruit, often large and globose, oblong, or conical, sometimes elongated, slender, striped, and serpentlike. 7. angina and 7. colubrina are known as snake-gourd or viper-gourd, also as snake-cucumber (which see, under ewewmber).

trichoschisis.c: trichoschisis (trik-os-ki’sis), n. [NL., < Gr. Opié (Tpix-), hair, + oyiow, a cleaving, < oiler, cleave: see schism.] Splitting of the hair.

trichoscolices.c: Trichoscolices (trik’6-sk0-li’sez), n. pl. [NL., < Gr. Opié (rpty-), hair, + oxgang, a worm.] A superordinal division, proposed in 1877 by Hux- ley to be established to include the Trematoda, Cestoidea, Turbellaria, and Rotifera, in order to discriminate the morphological type which they exemplify from that of the Nematoscolices, containing the Nematoidea. See Nematoscolices.

trichosis.c: trichosis (tri-ko’sis), m. [NL., < Gr. Opig (rpvyx-), hair, + -osis.] Any disease of the hair: same as plica, 1.

trichosomata.c: Trichosomata (trik-6-s0’ma-ta),. pl. [NL. (Diesing), < Gr. Opié (rpty-), hair, + odya(r-), the body.]_ The Peridinidz and allied infuse- rians, corresponding to the Choanoflagellata of H. J. Clark and W.S8..Kent. ~

trichosomatous.c: trichosomatous (trik-d-som’a-tus), a. Pertaining to the Trichosomata, or having their characters; having the body flagellate, as an infusorian.

trichosporange.c: trichosporange (trik-d-sp0’ranj), n. [< NL. trichosporangium, q.v.] In bot., same as trichosporangium. a

trichosporangium.c: trichosporangium (trik’6-sp6-ran’ji-um), n.; pl. trichosporangial (-ii). [NL. (Thuret), < Gr. Opi (Tptx-), hair, + NL. sporangium, q. v.) In bot., the plurilocular sporangium, or zodsporan- gium, of the fucoid algee, consisting of an aggregation of small cells, each one of which contains a single zoospore. Compare oosporangium.

trichostema.c: Trichostema (trik-6-sté’mi), m. [NL. (Lin- nus, 1763), named from the capillary filaments; < Gr. Opig (rpix-), hair, + orjua, stamen.] A genus of gamopetalous plants, of the order Labiate and tribe Ajugoidesx. It is characterized by the four long-exserted stamens with divaricate anther-cells, and by the deeply lobed ovary. The 8 species are allnatives of North America. They areclammy glandular herbs with a strong balsamic odor. They bear entire leaves, and axillary whorls of numerous mostly blue flowers, the corolla with a slender tube and nearly equally fivetoothed spreading border, from which the conspicuous arching stamens project, suggesting the popular name bluecurls (which see). The species of the eastern United States have a very strongly two-lipped and depressed calyx, and loose flower-clusters, as 7. dichotomum, the bastard pennyroyal. The western have the calyx normal and the flower-clusters dense. 7. lanatum, with a striking purple- woolly spike, is known in California as black sage.

trichosyphilis.c: trichosyphilis (trik-0-sif’i-lis), n. [NL., < Gr. Opié (Tptx-), hair, + NL. syphilis.) A syphilitic disease of the hair, —

tricircular.c: tricircular (tri-sér’ki-lir), a. Referring to three circles.—Tricircular coordinates, homogeneous point-codrdinates for a plane, each of which is equal to the power of the point relatively to a fixed coordinate circle divided by the radius of the circle. A linear equation ‘in such coordinates expresses a circle orthogonal to the “radical circle” which is orthogonal to the three cover- dinate circles; a quadric equation expresses a bicircular quartic; etc.—Tricircular geometry, geometry treated by means of tricircular coordinates. trick! (tri), v. [(a) Prob. an altered form, reverting to the orig. unassibilated form, of trich (mod. E. prop. spelled *twitch), < ME. tri- chen, triechen (also perhaps unassibilated * trick- en), < OF. richer, trickier, techier (also perhaps unassibilated *triquet, *tricquer), deceive, trick (ef. Pr. tric, deceit), = It. treccare, cheat, <L. tricar, ML. also tricare, trifle, act deceitfully, < trice, trifles, toys (see trich, treacher, treachery; ef. trick1, n., in the sense of ‘trifle, toy’); (6) the word, as a noun, being appar. influenced by, if not in part derived from, MD. trick, D. trek, a trick (een slime trek, a cunning trick, demand eenen trek speelen, play one a trick, etc.), a word not having the orig. meaning of ‘trick’ or ‘deceit,’ but a particular use of MD. trick, D. trek, a pull, draft, tug, line, < MD. trecken, D. trekken, draw: see trick?, and ef. track. Cf. F. trigaud, crafty, artful, cunning, trigauderie, a sly trick. The words spelled trick have been confused in popular apprehension and in the dictionaries, and the senses are entangled. See trick?, trick3, trick4.] I. trans. 1. To deceive by trickery; cozen; cheat. To be wrapt soft and warm in fortune’s smock When she... is pleased to trick or tromp mankind. B. Jonson, New Inn, i. 1. He was tricked out of the money while he was writing a receipt for it, and sent away without a farthing. Vanbrugh, Journey to London, iv. 1. 2. To bring, render, or induce by trickery; beguile; inveigle; cajole. rate They were thus tricked of their present. Bacon, Physical Fables, ii. trick Several members of Congress had previously complained that the demonetization scheme of 1873 had been pushed surreptitiously through the courses of its passage, Congress haying been tricked into accepting it, doing it scarcely knew what. W. Wilson, Cong. Gov., iii. : II. intrans. 1. To use trickery, deception, or imposture. Thus they jog on, still tricking, never thriving, And murdering plays, which still they call reviving. ; Dryden, To Granville. 2. To juggle; play. We may trick with the word life in its dozen senses until we are weary of tricking,... but one fact remains true throughout,... that we do not, properly speaking, love life at all, but living. R. L. Stevenson, Ais Triplex. St. To toy; handle idly. The muses forbid that I should restrain your meddling, whom I see already busy with the title and tricking over the leaves. B. Jonson, Catiline, To the Reader. trick! (tri), ». [< trick1, v.; prob. in part < MD. trick, D. trek, a trick, a pull, draft, etc.: see trick1, v., and cf. track.] 1. A crafty or fraudulent device; a deceitful expedient; an artifice; a stratagem. - There is some ¢rick in this, and you must know it, And be an agent too. Fletcher, Humorous Lieutenant, iv. 2. But you see they have some tricks to cousin God, as before to cousin the Diuell. Purchas, Pilgrimage, p. 213. O, the rare tricks of a Machiavelian! Webster, White Devil, v. 1. 2. A feat or an exhibition of skill or dexterity, as in juggling or sleight of hand. He can do tricks with his toes, wind silk and thread pearl with them. B. Jonson, Pan’s Anniversary. Entertain any puppy that comes, like a tumbler, with the same tricks over and over. Congreve, Old Batchelor, i. 4. 8. A roguish or mischievous performance; a prank; a practical joke; a hoax. _ If I be served such another trick, I'll have my brains ta’en out and buttered, and give them to a dog for a new-year's gift. Shak., M. W. of W.., iii. 5. 7. To play a trick and make some one or other look foolish was held the most pointed form of wit throughout the back regions of the manor. George Eliot, Felix Holt, xii. 4. A foolish, vicious, or disgraceful act: with disparaging or contemptuous force. Didst thou ever see me do such a trick? Shak., T. G. of V., iv. 4. 43. I hope you don’t mean to forsake it; that will be but a kind of a mongrel cur’s trick. Congreve, Old Batchelor, iv. 5. 5. A peculiar art; skill; adroitness; knack. Here’s fine revolution, an we had the trick to see’t. Shak., Hamlet, v. 1. 99. In a little while the trick of walking on the edge of the water close to the side wall had been learned. The Century, XXXIX. 220. 6. A peculiar trait, manner, habit, or practice; a characteristic; a peculiarity; a mannerism. In you a wildness is a noble trick, And cherish’d in ye, and all men must love it. Fletcher and Rowley, Maid in the Mill, iii. 2. What shall I say of the manifold and strange fashions of the garments that are used nowadays?... Sometime we follow the fashion of the Frenchmen. Another time we will have a trick of the Spaniards. Becon, Early Writings (ed. Parker Soc.), p. 204. We've a trick, we young fellows, you may have been told, Of talking (in public) as if we were old. 0. W. Holmes, The Boys. 7. A trace; a suggestion; a reminder. He hath a trick of Coeur-de-lion’s face. Shak., K. John, i. 1. 85. 8. Something pretended or unreal; a semblance; an illusion. Truth itself is in her head as dull And useless as a candle in a scull, And all her love of God a groundless claim, A trick upon the canvas, painted flame. Cowper, Conversation, 1. 782. In this poor trick of paint You see the semblance, incomplete and faint, Of the two-fronted Future. Whittier, The Panorama. trick-dagger (trik’dag’ér), n. 9. Any small article; a toy; a knickknack; a trifle; a trap; a mere nothing: sometimes ap- tricker! (trik’ér), n. plied to a child. [Obsolete or provincial U. S.] Why, ‘tis a cockle or a walnut-shell, A knack, a toy, a trick, a baby’s cap. Shak., T. of the S., iv. 3. 67. The women of this country were about an hundredth tricks and trifles about them. Hakluyt’s Voyages, II. 64. Camp tricks should be kept in their places, not thrown shelter skelter, or left lying where last used. Sportsman's Gazetteer, p. 640. Vainly the mother tried to hush the child; the prisoner called out, “Gimme the little trick, Sis; she jer wants to get th me.” The Century, XL. 219, 10. Incard-playing, the cards collectively which are played in one round. In whist and many other card-games the number of tricks taken makes up the score a by iis tricker?t, n.

trickerlock.c: tricker-lock (trik’ér-lok), ». beg 6471 on which the winning or losing of the game depends. A whet Aric is complete when the cards are turned and quitted. (tri), v.¢ [Prob. another use of trick], v., aS derived from the noun in the sense ‘a dexterous artifice,’ or ‘a touch.’ Cf. also trick4. For he [Cato] found not his Country... utterly destroyed, but tossed in a dangerous tempest; and being not of authority like the Pilot to take the sterne in hand, and govern the ship, he took himself to tricking the sails, and preparing the tackle, so to assist men of greater power. A country playhouse, some rude barn Tricked out for that proud use. Wordsworth, Prelude, vii. trick? (tri), v. t. trickery.c: trickery (trik’ér-i), n. [« trick + -eral. Cf. treachery (ME. tricherie, < OF. tricherie, etc.).] The practice of tricks or deceits; artifice; imposture. * tricking? (trik’ing), n.

trickle.c: trickle (trik’1), v.; pret. and pp. trickled, ppr. trickling. In mod. times the word has been regarded as connected with trill. Cf. Se. trinkle, also trintle, trickle.] I, intrans. 1. To flow in a small interrupted stream; run down in drops: as, water trickles from the eaves. The red blade triklond to his knee. MS. Cantab. Ff. v. 48, f. 122. (Halliwell.) Nay! ful of sorowe thou now me seest; The terris triiilen down on my face, For ‘‘filius regis mortuus est.” Political Poems, etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 207. 2. To let fall a liquidin drops or small broken streams; drip. H, James, Jr., Little Tour, p. 121. 8. To pass or flow gently like a small stream. How fluent nonsense trickles from his tongue! Pope, Dunciad, iii. 201. II. trans. To cause to trickle; pour or shed in small, slow streams. With adroit and tender hands they aided the doctor, and trickled stimulants down her throat. C. Reade, Hard Cash, xxxvii.

triclinium.c: triclinium (tri-klin’i-um), ». [< L. triclinium, <¢ Gr. tpixAiviov, also TpikAcvoc, a dining-room with three couches, < TpixAcvoc, with three couches, < tpeic (Tpl-), three, + KAivy, a couch: see clinic.] Among the Romans, the dining-room where guests were received, furnished with three couches, which occupied three sides of the din- ner-table, the fourth side being left open for the free ingress and egress of servants. On these couches, which also received the name of triclinium, the guests reclined at dinner or supper. Each couch usually accommodated three persons, and thus nine were as many as could take a meal together. The persons while taking their food lay very nearly flat on their breasts. See accubation.

tricoloredtricolored.c: tricolored, tricolored (tri’kul-ord), a. [< tricolor + -ed?.] Having three colors: as, a tricolored flag.—Tricolored violet, the pansy.

tricolortricolour.c: tricolor, tricolour (tri’kul-or),a.andn. [<F. tricolor = Sp. tricolor (ef. Pg. tricolored), < L. *tricolor, three-colored, < tres (tri-), three, + color, color.) I, a. Three-colored; tricolored: in zoology correlated with bicolor and unicolor. The Militia... added to the two colours of the Parisian cockade—red and blue— white, the colour which was that of the king. This was the tricolour cockade adopted on July 26, 1789. N. and Q., 7th ser., X. 157. II, x. A flag composed of three colors in large masses equal or nearly equal, as the national flags of Italy and Mexico; especially, the flag of France adopted during the Revolution, consisting of three equal parts — blue next the mast, red at the fly, and white between, or, in heraldic language, palewise of three pieces, azure, argent, and gules. The red and blue represented the colors of the city of Paris. We talk of... the lilies and tricolor of France. Preble, Hist. Flag, p. 3.

triconodon.c: Triconodon (tri-kon’6-don), n. [NL.: see triconodont.] A genus of mammals of the Purbeck beds in England, typical of the family Tr7- conodontide. T. mordax is a species founded on a mandibular ramus about 14 inches long.

They have molars with three stout erect cusps each, and a strong internal cingulum, stout canines, and semipro- recumbent or erect incisors. Cn.

tricoteuses.c: Tricoteuses (tre-ko-tez'), Les. [F.,‘the knitters.’] A class of women who frequented the tribunals and places of execution during the French Revolution, and sat knitting while they expressed their approval or disapproval of the turn of events. From their violence they have received the name of “Furies of the Guillotine.” They were not seen after 1794. Tricoupis. See Trikoupis. Tridentine Council. See Trent, Council of.

tricuspid.c: tricuspid (tri-kus’pid), a.andn. [= F. tricks- side, < L. tricuspid (tricuspid-), having three points, < tres (tri-), three, + cuspis, point: see cusp.] I, a. Having three cusps or points: specifically noting the valvular arrangement in the right ventricle of the heart, guarding the auriculoventricular orifice, in distinction from the bicuspid (or mitral) valves in the left ventricle. This valve consists of three segments, or there are three valves, of a triangular or trapezoidal shape, each formed by a fold of the lining membrane of the heart, and strengthened by a layer of fibrous tissue which may also contain contractile fibers. See cut I. under heart.— Tricuspid murmur, in pathol., murmur heard in tricuspid valvular disease.— Tricuspid teeth. See tooth.— Tricuspid valvular disease, disease of the tricuspid valve. II, ». 1. A tricuspid valve of the heart.— 2. A tricuspid tooth: correlated with bicuspid and multicuspid.

tricycle.c: tricycle (tri’si-kl), n. [< F. tricycle, < Gr. tisic (tpi-), three, + KvKAoc, circle, wheel.] A three-wheeled vehicle. Specifically —(at) A three-wheeled coach. See the quotation. Tricycles.—Christmas Day was rendered memorable to the Parisians by the starting of this new species of carriage for public accommodation. The tricycle is a kind of coach, mounted on three wheels; itis drawn by two horses only. It moves very lightly, although there is an appearance of weight about it. One wheel is placed exactly as the leading wheel.of the steam coach; it is capable of containing twenty persons, whom it conveys distances of at least three miles for five sous each. Annual Register for 1828 (‘‘ Chronicle,” p. 185), quoted {in N. and Q., 7th ser., X. 148. (b) A modification of the velocipede or bicycle, having three wheels. The wheels are variously arranged, as two Tricycle. a, driving-wheel, and 4, steering-wheels—all provided with solid rubber tires; ¢, frame; a, d’, sprocket-wheels; ¢, driving-chain working on the sprocket-wheels; /, cranks and pedals; g, saddle;%, cradle-spring, upon which the saddle is mounted; 7, handlebars for steering. in front and one behind, or the reverse. Tricycles are made for one or two persons; in the latter case the riders sit either side by side or one before the other. Compare bicycle.

tricycle (tri’si-kl), vi.; pret. and pp. tricycled, ppr. tricycling. [< tricycle, n.] To ride on a tricycle. [Recent.] I have heard the uninitiated say that tricycling must be so easy, just like working the velocipedes of our childhood. J.and E. R. Pennell, Canterbury Pilgrimage ona Tricycle.

tridacna.c: Tridacna (tri-dak’ni),n. [NL. (Da Costa, 1776), also erroneously Tridachia, Tridachna, Tridach- ‘nes; < Gr. Tpidaxvoc, eaten at three bites, < zpeic (pl-), three, + daxvew, bite.] A genus of inequilateral equivalve bivalve mollusks, forming the type of the family Tridacnidz. The margin is deeply waved and indented, the opposite sides fitting Shell of one of the Giant Clams (7vzdacna squamosa). into each other. 1. gigas, the largest bivalve shell known, attains a length of 2 or 3 feet and a weight of 500 pounds ormore. The animal may weigh 20 pounds or more. It is a native of the East Indian seas, and is edible. The great valves are used for various purposes, as for baptismal fonts, as receptacles for holy water, and, it is alleged, as babies’ bathtubs. The substance of the shell is extremely hard, and calcification progresses until almost every trace of organic structure is obliterated. Pieces of the shell weighing 7 or 8 pounds are used by the natives of the Caroline Islands for axes. The other species of the genus, as 7. sguamosa and T. crocia, are much smaller. Also called Pelex. See also cut under Tridacnide.

tride.c: tride (trid), a. [< F. tride, lively, cadenced; origin obscure.] In hunting, short and swift; fleet: as, a tride pace. Tride, a word signifying short and swift. A tride-pace is a going of short and swift motions. A horse is said to work tride upon volts when the times he makes with his haunches are short and ready. Some apply the word only to the motion of the haunches. Osbaldiston, Sportsman’s Dict., p. 635.

trident.c: trident (tri’denz), n. [L.: see trident.} A three-toothed or three-bladed implement or weapon. In the latter example [a halberd] the axe-blade being balanced by atridens. J. Hewitt, Anc. Armour, IT. 269.

trident (tri’dent), n. [= F. trident = Sp. Pg. It. trident, < LL. triden(t-)s, three-toothed, three-pronged; as noun, a three-pronged spear, a trident as an attribute of Neptune; < tres (tri-), three, + den(t-)s = E. tooth: see tooth.] 1. Any instrument of the form of a fork with three prongs; specifically, a three-pronged fishspear. —2. A spear with three prongs, usually barb-pointed, forming a characteristic attribute of Poseidon (Neptune), the sea-god. See also cut under Poseidon. His nature is too noble for the world: He would not flatter Neptune for his trident, Or Jove for’s power to thunder. Shak., Cor., iii. 1. 256. 3. Hence, marine sovereignty; rule over the ocean or sea. To Worlds remote she wide extends her Reign, And wields the Trident of the stormy Main. Congreve, Birth of the Muse. 3 Trident.— Archaistic relief of Neptune, in the Vatican, tridiapason 4. In Rom. antiq., a three-pronged spear used by the retiarius in gladiatorial ecombats.—5. In geom., a crunodal plane cubic curve haying the line at infinity for one of the tangents at the node. It was discovered and named by Descartes. tridental} (tri-den’tal), a. ([ trident + -al.} Of or pertaining to a trident; in the form of a trident; possessing or wielding a trident. The white-mouth’d water now usurps the shore, And scorns the pow’r of her tridental guide. Quarles, Emblems, i. 2. Trident, s. Nor Juno less endured, when erst the bold Son of Amphitryon with tridental shaft Her bosom pierced. Cowper, Iliad, v. 458.

tridentate.c: tridentate (tri-den’tat), a. [= F. trident, < NL, *tridentatus, having three teeth, < L. tres (tri-), three, + dentatus, toothed: see dentate, and ef. trident.) Having three teeth or toothlike parts; tridentated; three-pronged.

tridented.c: tridented (tri-den’ted), a. [< trident + -ed2.] Having three teeth or prongs. Neptune... Held his tridented mace. Quarles, Hist. Jonah, § 6.

tridentiferous.c: tridentiferous (tri-den-tif’e-rus), a. [< L. wi- identifer, < triden(t-)s, a trident, + ferre = EH. bear.] Bearing a trident. Bailey, 1727.

tridentine.c: Tridentine (tri-den’tin), a. and. [< NL. Tri- dentinus, < ML. Tridentum, Trent (see def.).] I, a. 1. Pertaining to Trent, a city of Tyrol, or to the Council of Trent (1545-63): as, Tridentine decrees (that is, the decrees of the Council of Trent, the authoritative symbol of the Roman Catholic Church); Tridentine theology (that is, theology in accordance with those decrees, Roman Catholic theology). The King [Henry VIII.] remained a believer in Roman Catholic forms of doctrine; but... those forms had not yet, by the Tridentine decrees, been hardened into their later inflexibility. Stubbs, Medieval and Modern Hist., p 261. 2. Conforming to the Council of Trent, or its decrees and doctrine. Her [Elizabeth’s] explanation of her supreme governorship might have satisfied every one but the most Tridentine papist, but she re-enacted the most stringent part of her father’s act of supremacy. Stubbs, Medieval and Modern Hist., p. 324. Tridentine catechism. See catechism, 2. II. x. A Roman Catholic: a name implying that the present system of Roman Catholic doctrine and practice dates from the Council of Trent (1545). The creeds of the Roman Catholic Church are four in number—the Apostles’, the Nicene, the Athanasian, and the Creed of Pope Pius IV. The last named is also called the Profession of the Tridentine Faith. It was formulated in 1564, and includes the Nicene Creed, summary of the doctrines defined by the Council of Trent, a recognition of the Roman Church as mother and teacher of all churches, and an oath of obedience to the Pope as successor of St. Peter and vicar of Christ. With the addition of the doctrines of the immaculate conception (promulgated in 1854) and the papal infallibility (defined in 1870), this creed is that which must be accepted by converts to the Roman Church, except those from the Greek Church (for whom special forms are provided), and is incumbent on all Roman Catholic priests and teachers. They called the council of Chalcedon a ‘‘council of fools,” and styled the Catholics Chalcedonians, just as Anglicans have styled Catholics of the present day Tridentines. Dublin Rev. (Imp. Dict.)

tridentipes.c: Tridentipes (tri-den’ti-péz), n. [NlL. (Hitch- cock, 1858), < L. tres (tri-), three, + dens (dent-) = E. tooth, + pes = E. foot.) A genus of gigantic animals, formerly supposed to be birds, now believed to be dinosaurian reptiles, known by their footprints in the Triassic formation of the Connecticut valley.

triene.c: triene (tri’én),. [< NL. trina, <¢ Gr. rpiava, a three-pronged fishspear, a three-pronged fork, a trident, < rpeic (pi-), three: see three. | Among sponge-spicules, a cladose rhabdus which bears at one end three secondary rays or eadi diverging at equal angles from one another. Various modifications of the trizene have received specific names. A trieene with recurved arms like a grapnel is an anatrizne; with porrect arms, a protrizne; with arms at right angles with the shaft, an orthotrizne; with bifurcate arms, a dichotrizne; with trifurcate, a trichotriene. triennial.c: triennial (tri-en’i-al), a. and m. [< L. as if *triennialis, < triennium, a period of three years, < tres (tri-), three, + annus, year: see annual. Cf. triennal.] I, a. 1. Continuing three years: 6474 as, triennial parliaments; specifically, of plants, lasting or enduring for three years. There are that hold the elders should be perpetual: there are others for a triennial, others for a biennial eldership. Bp. Hall, Episcopacy by Divine Right, iii. § 5. 2. Happening every three years. The triennial election of senators. The Century, XXXVII. 871. Triennial abbot. See abbot.—Triennial Act, an English statute of 1694 which required that a new Parliament be summoned at least once in three years, and that no Parliament be continued more than three years. It was repealed by the Septennial Act, in 1716.—Triennial prescription, in Scots law, a limit of three years within which creditors can bring actions for certain classes of debts, such as merchants’ and tradesmen’s accounts, servants’ wages, house rents (when under verbal lease), and debts due to lawyers or doctors. II. n. 1. A mass performed daily for three years for the soul of a dead person.— 2, A plant which continues to live for three years.—38. triennialact.c: Triennial Act (tri-en'i-al at). In English his¬ tory, an act of Parliament, passed in 1094, which limited the duration of Parliaments to three years, and forbade a period of three years to pass without the summoning of a Parliament. It was superseded by the Septennial Act of 1710.
