typhlophthalmi.c: Typhlophthalmi (tif-lof-thal/mi),. pl. [NL., < Gr. ruddoc¢, blind, + opfaApudc, eye.] In Cope’s classification, a superfamily of pleurodont lizards, represented by the Anelytropide, Aconti- idz, and Aniellide.

typhlophthalmic.c: typhlophthalmic (tif-lof-thal’mik), a. [< Typh- lophthalmi + -ic.] Of or pertaining to the Typhlophthalmi.

typhlopide.c: Typhlopide (tif-lop’i-dé),». pl. [NL., < Typhlops + -idz.] A family of angiostomatous scole- ophidian serpents, typified by the genus Typhlops ; the worm-snakes or blindworm. It formerly included all the small serpents with the mouth not distensible and teeth only in one jaw, upper or lower, being the same as T'yphlopoidea. By the division of these into two families, Catodonta and Hpanodonta, with lower and with upper teeth only, respectively, the Typhlopide are restricted to the latter, and contrasted with Stenostomidz.

typhlopoidea.c: Typhlopoidea (tif-l6-poi’dé-%), n. pl. [NL., < Gr. tugAde, blind, + ow, eye, + eidos, form.] A suborder of Ophidia, containing the small seolecophidian or angiostomatous snakes of the families Typhlopide and Stenostomatide, and thus equivalent to Typhlopide in a broad sense. They differ from all other ophidians in having no transverse bone of the skull, the pterygoid disconnected from the quadrate, the palatines with their long axes transverse and bounding the nasal choate behind, and the ethmoturbinal forming part of the roof of the mouth. Typhlops (tif/lops), x. [NL. (Schneider), < Gr. TuoAoy, blind, < ru@Adc, blind, + ow, eye.] The typical genus of Typhlopidz, having the muzzle covered above with rostral and internasal scutes, and one ocular, one preocular, and one nasal plate.

typhlops.c: typhlops (tif/lop), n. [< NL. Zyphlops.] A small snake of the family Typhlopide; aworm- snake or blindworm.;

typhlosis.c: typhlosis (tif-lo’sis), m. [NL., < Gr. riddwore, a making blind, blindness, ¢ rvdA0vv, make blind, < rvd/6c, blind.] Blindness.

typhlosolar.c: typhlosolar (tif-l0-s0’lir), a. [< typhlosole + -ar3.] Of the character of or pertaining to a typhlosole. Micros. Sci., N. S., XX VII. 565.

typhlosole.c: typhlosole (tif’l6-s6l), ». [< Gr. rv@Aédc, blind, + cory, tube, pipe: see solen.] A thick folding of the intestine of certain annelids, mollusks, etc., formed by the involution of the wall of the intestine along the dorsomedian line, and projecting into the intestinal cavity. Husaley, Anat. Invert., p. 196.

typhoan.c: Typhoéan (ti-fo’é-an), a. [Also, erroneously, Typhean, Typhean; < L. Typhoeus, ¢ Gr. Tudwete, contr. Tvddc, Typhoéus (see def.); ef. Typhon?.] Of, pertaining to, or resembling Typhoéus (or Typhos), a monster of Greek mythology, who tried to conquer the gods, but was overcome by Zeus and buried under Mount Etna. Typhoéus is described as vomiting flame from a hundred mouths, and thus typifies a volcano.

typhoid.c: typhoid (tif’loid), a. [< Gr. rv@ddc, blind, + eld¢, form.] Having defective vision, as a blindworm.

typhoid (ti’foid),a.andm. [= F. typhoid, < Gr. *rvdoednc, contr. Tvdadyc, delirious, of persons suffering from fever, also of the fever itself, < rupoc, smoke, also stupor arising from fever: see typhus.] I, a. Resembling typhus: noting a specific continued fever.—Bilious typhoid fever. See feverl.—_Typhoid bacillus, or Eberth’s bacillus, a microorganism found in the intestinal ulcers, and elsewhere in the bodies, of those dying from typhoid fever, and believed to be the cause of this disease.— Typhoid condition or state, a condition occurring sometimes in the course of acute diseases of a depressing type, in which there is marked lowering of all the vital forces, shown by prostration, muttering delirium, carphologia, muscular twitchings, unconscious discharges from the bladder and bowels, a dry, cracked, often blackish tongue, etc.—Ty- phoid fever. See fever1.—Typhoid pneumonia, See pneumonia. II.. Typhoid fever. See fever.

typhoidal.c: typhoidal (ti’foi-dal), a. [< typhoid + -al.] Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of typhoid fever: as, typhoidal symptoms.

typhomalarial.c: typhomalarial (ti’fo-ma-la’ri-al), a. [« ty- pho(id) + malarial.| Involving both typhoid and malarial characters: applied to a disease caused by the combined influence of filth and the malarial poison, or a typhoid fever in which the symptoms are modified by the action of malaria. Whether either of these conditions exists has been a subject of dispute among medical writers.

typhomania.c: typhomania (ti-fo-ma’ni-&), n. [< Gr. ridoc, stupor (see typhus, typhoid), + pavia, madness. } typhomania A low, muttering delirium with stupor, but without sleep, as seen in severe cases of typhus fever. Also typhonia. typhon!t (ti’fon), n. [< NL. typhon (Bacon), < Gr. Tvdav, also Tuddc, a furious whirlwind; ef. Tvgov, Typhon, one of the giants, son of Typhoeus, and Tvdac, Tudweic, father of Typhon, and a god of the winds; ef. ridoc, cloud, smoke, mist, < ridevy, smoke; ef. Skt. dhiipa, smoke. Cf. typhus. The word has been merged in typhoon, q. v.} A whirlwind. Typhon? (ti’fon), n. [< L. Typhon, < Gr. Tudar, one of the giants: see def. and typhonl.] 1. In Gr. myth., a son of Typhoéus, and the father of the winds: later confused with Typhos or Typhoéus.— 2, The Greek name of the Egyptian divinity Set, the personification of the principle of evil.—8. [/. c.] A large East Indian heron, Ardea sumatrana.

typhon.c: Typhon (ti'fon). [Gr. T vtyauv.] 1. In Greek mythology, a son of Typhoeus, and the father of the winds: later confused with Typlios or Typhoeus. — 2. In Egyptian mythology: see Set.

typhonia.c: typhonia (ti-fo’ni-i), m [NL., < Gr. ridoc, stupor: see typhus.] Same as typhomania.

typhonic.c: typhonic (ti-fon’ik), a. [< typhon1 + -ic.] Of or pertaining to a typhon or typhoon; having the force or character of a typhoon.

typhoon.c: typhoon (ti-fon’),. [Formerly also tyfoon; altered, in simulation of typhon1, from the earlier

typhotoxin.c: typhotoxin (ti-fo-tok’sin), ». [< Gr. ridoc, stupor (see typhus), + ro&(«xdv), poison, + -in?.] A toxin (C7H;7NOg) obtained from cultures of the bacillus of typhoid fever.

typhous.c: typhous (ti’‘fus), a. [< typhus) + -ous.] Of or relating to typhus.

typhpoison.c: typh-poison (tif’poi’zn), n. [< typhus), ty- ph(oid), + poison.) Poison or virus which when admitted into the system produces typh-fever, or continued low fevers, as typhus or typhoid.

typhus.c: typhus (ti’fus), ». [= F. typhus = Sp. tiro = Pg. typo = It. tiro = D. G. typhus = Sw. Dan. tyfus, < NL. typhus, typhus (ef. L. typhus, pride, vanity), ¢ Gr. rigor, smoke, vapor, mist (hence, vanity, conceit), also stupor, esp. stupor arising from fever, < Tide, smoke: see typhonl.] A fever accompanied by great prostration, usually delirium, and an eruption of small reddish-purple spots; ship-fever; jailfever. Compare typhus fever, under fever.—Abdominal typhus fever. See fever.— Malignant bilious typhus fever. See fever!.—Surgical typhus fever, pyemia.— Typhus abdominalis, typhoid fever. See fever1.—Typhus am- bulatorius, walking typhoid fever.—Typhus carce- rum, jail-fever.—Typhus castrensis, camp-fever. See Jever1.—Typhus exanthematicus, typhus fever.— Typhus fever. See def. and fever1.__T typhus gangliaris, typhoid fever.—Typhus icterode, yellow fever. See Jever!.—Typhus petechialis, typhus fever.— Typhus recurrent, relapsing fever. ‘

typic.c: typic (tip’ik), a. [= F. typique = Sp. tipico = g. typico (ef. D. G. typisch = Sw. Dan. typist), < L. typicum, < Gr. ruixée, of or pertaining to a type, conformable, typical, < rizoc, impression, type: see type.] Constituting or representing a type; typical. [Rare.] 6564 Thou Gracious deign’st to let the fair One view Her Typic People. Prior, Second Hymn of Callimachus. Here’s Smith already swearing at my feet That I’m the typic she. Away with Smith! Mrs. Browning, Aurora Leigh, ix. Typic fever, a fever that is regular in its attacks, or that follows a particular type: opposed to erratic fever.

typical.c: typical (tip’i-kal), a. [< LL. typicalis, < L. typicum, typic: see typic and -al.] 1. Having the character of a significant or symbolic type; serving as an index or a symbol of something past, present, or to come; representative; emblematic; illustrative. The description is, as sorted best to the apprehension of those times, typical and shadowier. Milton, Church-Government, i. 2. On the right hand of Popery sat Judaism, represented by an old man embroidered with phylacteries, and distinguished by many typical figures, which I had not skill enough to unriddle. Addison, Tatler, No. 257. Typical remains of every disposition must continue traceable even to the remotest future. H. Spencer, Social Statics, p. 329. 2. Constituting or conforming to a type or pattern; representative in kind or quality; serving as a characteristic example of a group or an aggregate: as, a typical animal, plant, species, or genus; a typical building; typical conduct. Also typal. Compare atypical, etypical, subtypical. I need hardly name David and Jonathan; yet I cannot pass them by; for theirs is, and will remain, the typical friendship of the world. N. A. Rev., CKX XIX. 455. 3. Of or pertaining to a type or types; significantly characteristic or illustrative; indicative; connotative: as, a typical example or specimen; typical markings, colors, or limbs.—Typical cells, in bot., same as fundamental cells (which see, under fundamental).

typicality.c: typicality (tip-i-kal’i-ti), n. [« typical + -ity.] The fact or state of being typical; existence as a type or symbol; also, adherence to types or standards. [Rare.] Such men... have spurned the empty typicality of the church whenever she has pretended to appease that immortal want [of a really divine righteousness]. ‘ H. James, Subs. and Shad., p. 222.

typically.c: typically (tip’i-kal-i), adv. In a typical manner; representatively; symbolically. Other Levitical lambs took away sin typically, this really. Rev. T. Adams, Works, II. 113. In the Eucharist he [Christ] still is figured... more clearly, but yet still but typically, or in figure. Jer. Taylor, Dissuasive from Popery, II. ii. § 3.

typicum.c: typicum (tip’i-kum), ». [< MGr. rumxdv, a book of ritual, an imperial decree, neut. of Gr. rum- Koc, of or pertaining to a type: see typic.] In the Gr. Ch., same as directory, 1.

typidentata.c: Typidentata (ti’pi-den-ta’tii), n. pl. [NL., < L. typus, type, + dentatus, toothed.] A division of placental mammals, containing all excepting the Edentata.

typification.c: typification (tip/i-fi-ka’shon), n. [< typify + -ic-at-ion.] The act or state of typifying.

typifier.c: typifier (tip’i-fi-éer),n. [< typify + -erl.] One who or that which typifies. A modern typifier, who deals only in similitude and correspondences. Warburton, Works, XI. 403.

typify.c: typify (tip’i-fi), v. ¢.; pret. and pp. typified, ppr. typifying. [< L. typus, type, + facere, make (see -fy).] 1. To represent by an image, form, model, or resemblance; show forth; prefigure. Our Saviour was typified indeed by the goat that was slain. Sir T. Browne, Vulg. Err. 2. To be or constitute a type of; embody the typical characteristics of; exemplify: as, the tiger typifies all the animals of the cat kind.

typist.c: typist (ti’pist), m. [< type + -ist.] One who uses a typewriter. [Recent.]

typocosmy.c: typocosmy (ti’pd-koz-mi), ». [< Gr. rio, type, + xéopoc, the world.} A representation of the world; universal terminology. [Rare.] Books of typocosmy, which have been made since; being nothing but amass of words of all arts, to give men countenance, that those which use the terms might be thought to understand the art. Bacon, Advancement of Learning, ii.

typodontia.c: Typodontia (ti-po-don’shiii), n. pl. [NL., < Gr. toroc, type, + dot¢ (ddovT-) = E. tooth.] In Blyth’s edition of Cuvier, an order of placental Mammalia, comprehending the Bimana, Quadrumana, and Carnaria (carnassiers) of Cuvier; one of two orders constituting Blyth’s zoépha- ous type of mammals. [Not in use.] o-etching (ti’pd-ech’ing), n. The process of making a plate for relief printing by etching t ——_, typtologist with acid the parts of the surface of a stone ~ which have not previously been protected. See lithography. Encye. Brit., XXTU. 704. typog. An abbreviation of typography or typographer.

typograph.c: typograph (ti’po- or tip’6-graf), n. [< Gr. siroc, type, + ypadia, < ypadew, write.] A type-mak- ing and typesetting machine. Science, VIII. 252.

typographer.c: typographer (ti-pog’ra-fér), n. [< typography A sc 1. One who prints with or from ree. or by typographic process. There is a very ancient edition of this work [Justinian’s “Tnstitutes”), without date, place, or typographer. T. Warton, Hist. Eng. Poetry, II. 381, note. 2. A beetle of the genus Bostrychus, as B. ty- pographicus: so called from the characteristic markings its larva makes on the bark of trees.

typographic.c: typographic (tip-0- or ti-po-graf’ik), a. [= F. typographique = Sp. tipografico = Pg. typogra- philo = It. tipografico; as typography + -ic.] Of or pertaining to the art of printing from types, woodcuts, or plates in -high relief.— Typographic machine, a machine for impressing a matrix from which a stereotype plate may be cast. It has keys which, as they are depressed, operate types in the order desired. EH. H. Knight.—Typographic point. See point, 14 (b).

typographical.c: typographical (tip-6- or ti-pd-graf’i-kal), a. [< typographic + -al.] 1. Of or pertaining to typography, or the use or manipulation of types for printing: as, typographical errors.— 2+. Em- blematie; figurative; typical.

typographically.c: typographically (tip-o- or ti-pd-graf’i-kal-i), adv. 1. By means of types; after the manner of -type-printers, as opposed to lithographic or copperplate methods.— 2}. Emblematically; figuratively.

typographist.c: typographist (ti-pog’ra-fist), m. [< typography + -ist.] A student of typography; a person concerned with the art or history of printing. Athenzum, No. 3282, p. 412. [Rare.]

typography.c: typography (ti-pog’ra-fi),n. [= F. typographie = Sp. tipografia = Pg. typographia = It. tipo- grafia = G. typographie = Sw. Dan. typografi, < Gr. rio, impression, type, + -ypadia, <ypagew, write.] 1. The art of composing types and printing from them. Caxton taught us typography about the year 1474. Johnson, Idler, No. 69. 2. In a restricted use, type-work; the branch of printing connected with composition; the preparation of matter in type for use in printing.— 8, The general character or appearance of printed matter.— 4+. Emblematical or hieroglyphic representation. Sir T. Browne, Vulg. rt

typolite.c: typolite (tip’6-lit), n. [< Gr. rimoc, impression, + Aifoc, stone.] A stone or petrifaction impressed with the figure of an animal ora plant; a fossil, in an ordinary paleontological sense.

typological.c: typological (tip-6- or ti-pd-loj’i-kal), a. [KX ty- polog-y + -ical.] Of or pertaining to typology; relating to types or symbols: as, typological exegesis. Encyc. Brit., XL. 606.

typology.c: typology (ti-pol’6-ji), n. [< Gr. rimoc, type, + -Aoyia, ¢ Aéyerv, speak: see -ology.] The doe- trine of types or symbols; a discourse on types, especially those of Scripture..

typomania.c: typomania (tip-0- or ti-po-ma’ni-&), m. [< Gr. Turoc, type, + pavia, madness.] A mania for the use of printing-types; a strong propensity to write for publication. [Humorous.] The slender intellectual endowments and limited vital resources which are so very frequently observed in association with typomania. O. W. Holmes, The Atlantic, LI. 66.

typonym.c: typonym (ti’po-nim), n. [< Gr. rio, type, + ovula, name.} In zool. and bot., a name based upon an indication of a type species or of a type specimen. Coues, The Auk (1884), VI. 321.

typonymic.c: typonymic (tip-6- or ti-po-nim’ik), a. [< typonym + -ic.] Named with reference to a type, as a genus whose type species is declared, or a species a type specimen of which is recorded. Coues, 1885.

typorama.c: typorama (tip-d- or ti-pd-ri’mii), m. [< Gr. ré- moc, type, + paua, view: see panorama.) A view of something consisting of a detailed plan ormodel; a representation in facsimile. [Rare.] The typorama, a plaster of Paris model of the Undercliff, Isle of Wight. First Year of a Silken Reign, p. 214.

typtological.c: typtological (tip-td-loj’i-kal), a. [< typtology + -ical.] Of or pertaining to typtology.

typtology.c: typtology (tip-tol’6-ji), n. [Irreg. < Gr. rimrew, strike, + -/oyia, < Aéyerv, speak: see -ology.] In spiritualism, the theory or practice of spirit- rapping; also, the key to spirit-rappings.

tyr.c: Tyr (tir),n. [Icel. Tyr: see Tiw, Tuesday.) In Northern myth., the god of war and victory, son of Odin. He is the same as the Anglo-Saxon Tiw. tyrant, ”. and v. tyranness} (ti’ran-es), n. female tyrant. And now the tyranness bears all the stroke, Clogging her suffering neck with servile yoke. Times’ Whistle (E. E. T. 8.), p. 92.

Tyr (sir). [ON. Tyr.] In Northern mythology, the god of war and victory, son of Odin. He is the same as the Anglo-Saxon Tiw. He is represented with one hand, the other having been bitten off by the wolf Fenris, in whose mouth he had placed it as a pledge. Tyrannic Love, or the Royal Martyr. A tragedy by Dryden, produced in 1668 or 1669, printed in 1670.

tyrannic.c: tyrannic (tivan’ik), a. [< F. tyrannique= Sp. tirdnico = Pg. tyrannic = It. tirannico, < L. tyrannicus, ML. tirannicus, < Gr. tvpavvixéc, of or pertaining to a tyrant, < ripavvoc, tyrant: see tyrant.| Same as tyrannical. Brute violence and proud tyrannic power. Milton, P. R., i. 218,

tyrannical.c: tyrannical (ti-ran’i-kal), a. [< tyrannic + -al.] 1. Having the character of a tyrant; acting like a tyrant; despotic in rule or procedure; arbitrary; imperious: as, a tyrannical master. —2. Pertaining to or characteristic of a tyrant; unjustly severe in operation; oppressive: as, a tyrannical government; tyrannical actions. In this point charge him home, that he affects Tyrannical power. Shak., Cor., iii. 3. 2. = Syn. Domineering, severe, oppressive, galling, grinding. See despotism.

tyrannically.c: tyrannically (ti-ran’i-kal-i), adv. In a tyrannical manner; with arbitrary or oppressive exercise of power. Shak., Hamlet, ii. 2. 356.

tyrannicidal.c: tyrannicidal (ti-ran’i-si-dal), a. [< tyrannicide + -al.] Relating to tyrannicide. tyrannicide! (ti-ran’i-sid), n. [< F. tyrannicide, < Li. tyrannicida, a slayer of a tyrant, < tyrannus, tyrant, + -ida, < cedere, slay.] One who kills a tyrant. Hear what Xenophon says in Hiero: ‘‘People... erect Statues in their Temples to the Honour of Tyrannicides.” Milton, Answer to Salmasius, v. tyrannicide? (ti-ran’i-sid), n. [< F. tyrannicide, < L. tyrannicidium, the slaying of a tyrant, < tyrannus, tyrant, + -cidium, < cedere, slay.] The act of killing a tyrant; the putting a tyrannical ruler to death on account of his acts.

tyrannide.c: Tyrannide (ti-ran’i-dé), v. pl. [NL., < Tyrannus + -idz.| A family of passerine birds, named from the genus Tyrannus; the tyrant-birds or tyrant-flyeatchers. There are many genera, and upward of 400 species, confined to America, and chiefly represented in the Neotropical region. They are readily distinguished by the nonoscine (clamatorial or mesomyodian) character of the syrinx, the scutelliplantar tarsi of the exaspidean type, ten primaries of which the first is not spurious, twelve rectrices, and the bill almost invariably hooked at the end by an overhanging point of the upper mandible. The rictus as a rule is strongly bristled; the hind toe is eleutherodactylus, or freely movable apart from the others (as in oscine Passeres), and the outer and middle toes are united only at their bases. Itisone of the most extensive and characteristic groups of its grade in the New World, only the Tanagridz and Trochilidz approaching it in these respects. Its relationships are with the other nonoscine Passeres highly developed in and peculiar to the Neotropical region, namely the Pipridz and Cotingide; but not with the true flycatchers, or Mus- cicadid#, to which many of the long-known species used to be referred. Only 8 or 9 genera extend into the United States, and of these only 5 (Tyrannus, Myiarchus, Sayornis, Contopus, and Empidonax) have any extensive distribution in that country. The genus Oxyrhynchus, without any hook of the beak, is often now separated as the type of another family; aside from this the Tyrannide are by Sclater divided into 4 subfamilies — Txniopterinz, Platy- rhynchine, Eleniine, and Tyrannine. See cuts under Contopus, Empidonax, Fluvicola, kingbird, Megarhynchus, Milwulus, pewit, Platyrhynchus, Pyrocephalus, Sayornis, scissortat, Txnioptera, Todirostr um, and Tyrannulus.

tyrannine.c: Tyrannine (tir-a-ni’né),. pl. [NL., < Tyrannus ~in.| A subfamily of Tyrannide, containing the true tyrant-flycatchers, of arboreal habits, and usually more or less extensively oliva- eeous coloration, sometimes gray, varied chiefly with white or yellow, and often with bright-colored spot on the crown. Birds of this group abound throughout the woodlands of America, from the limit of trees both north and south, and play an important part in the economy of nature, comparable to that of the true flycatchers (Muscicapide) of the Old World. In the United States the scissortail (Milvulus forficatus), the common kingbird or bee-martin (Tyrannus carolinensis), the great crested flycatcher (Myiarchus crinites), the pewit or water- pewee (Sayornis (or Empidias) fuscus), the wood-pewee or pheebe-bird (Contopus virens), and several smaller flycatchers of the genus Ympidonazx furnish characteristic examples of the Tyrannine. There are in all about 20 genera. An obsolete form of tyrant. [< tyran + -ess.] A 6565

tyrannine (tir’a-nin), a. [< Tyrannus + -ine.] Of or pertaining to the Tyrannine; relating to or resembling the genus Zyrannus: in a narrow sense applied to the larger tyrant-flycatchers, in distinction from the smaller tyrannuline forms.

tyranniscus.c: Tyranniscus (tir-a-nis’kus), n. [NL. (Cabanis and Heine, 1859), dim. of Tyrannus, q. v.] A genus of small tyrant-flycatchers, of the subfamily Hlzniine, containing about 11 species, ranging from Guatemala to southern Brazil, as T. nigricapillus and T. cinereiceps.

tyrannish.c: tyrannish (ti’ra-nish), a. [< ME. tyrannish, ti- rannish; <tyran + ~ish1.] Like a tyrant; characteristic of a tyrant; tyrannical. The proud tivannish Romain Tarquinius, which was than king. Gower, Conf. Amant., vii.

tyrannize.c: tyrannize (tir’a-niz), v.; pret. and pp. tyrannized, ppr. tyrannizing. [< F. tyranniser = Sp. tiramzar = Pg. tyrannizer = It. tirannizzare, < Gr. tupavvigerv, take the part of a tyrant, < tipavvoc, tyrant: see tyrant.) I. intrans. 1. To act as a tyrant; exercise tyrannical power; rule despotically or cruelly: used of persons, with over before an object. I made thee miserable, What time I threw the people’s suffrages On him that thus doth tyrannize o’er me. Shak., Vit. And., iv. 3. 20. Hence—2. To have a tyrannical influence; exercise oppressive restraint; maintain arbitrary control: used of things, commonly with over. Nor, while we trust in the mercy of God through Christ Jesus, [shall] fear be able to tyrannize over us. Hooker, Eccles. Polity, v. 47. The first and last lesson of the useful arts is that Nature tyrannizes over our works. Emerson, Art. TI. trans. 1. To rule, treat, or affect tyrannically; act the tyrant to or over. This is he that shal tyrannize the cities of Rome, and be the rhine of my house. Guevara, Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 164. They would enjoyne a slavish obedience without law, which is the known definition of a tyrant and a tyranniz’d people. Milton, Apology for Smectymnuus, 2+. To make tyrannically oppressive; convert into an instrument of tyranny. Boisterous edicts tyrannizing the blessed ordinance of marriage into the quality of a most unnatural and unchristianly yoke. Milton, Divorce, ii. 20. Also spelled tyrannise.

tyrannoid.c: tyrannoid (tir’a-noid), a. [< Tyrannus + -oid.] Resembling or related to a tyrant-bird; belonging to the Tyrannoidee.

tyrannoidee.c: Tyrannoidee (tir-a-noi’dé-é6), n. pl. [NL., ¢ Tyrannus + -oidex.| A superfamily of passerine birds, containing those families of Passeres which have a mesomyodian tracheobronchial syrinx and anindependently movable hallux, divided into Heteromeri and Homeomeri, according to the situation of the main artery of the thigh, and consisting of the families Xenicide (New Zealand), Philepittide (Madagascar), Pittide (Ethiopian, Oriental, and Australian), and the American Tyrannide, Pipride, Cotingid, and Phytotomide. Nine tenths of the species are American, and most of these Neotropical.

tyrannous.c: tyrannous (tir’a-nus), a. [< tyran + -ous.] Of tyrannical character or quality; given to or marked by tyranny; harshly despotic. And, like the tyrannous breathing of the north, Shakes all our buds from growing. Shak., Cymbeline, i. 3. 36. And now the storm-blast came, and he Was tyrannous and strong. Coleridge, Ancient Mariner, i.

tyrannously.c: tyrannously (tir’a-nus-li), adv. In a tyrannous manner; with tyrannical force or intent; despotically; cruelly. There, being both together in the loud, They each at other tyrannously flew. Spenser, F. Q., V. ii. 13. Julius before his Death tyrannously had made himself Emperor of the Roman Commonwealth. Milton, Hist. Eng., ii.

tyrannula.c: Tyrannula (ti-ran’i-li), n. [NL. (Swainson, 1827), dim. of Tyrannus, q. v.] 1. A genus of tyrannuline flycatchers, the type of which is T. barbata. Tt has been loosely used for many small olivaceous species now distributed in different genera. Owing to its similarity to the name Tyrannulus of prior date, it is now disused, the species properly belonging to Tyrannula being called Mytobius. 2. [l. c.] A small tyrant-flycatcher of the above or some related genus; a tyrannuline.

tyrannuline.c: tyrannuline (ti-ran’i-lin), a. and n. [¢ Ty- rannula + -ine.] I, a. Pertaining or related tyranny to the tyrannulas, or small tyrant-flyeatchers, as distinguished, from the larger or tyrannine forms. II. n. A little olivaceous flycatcher; a member of the genus Tyrannula, or some similar bird. They are such as those figured under Contopus, Empidonax, and pewit.

tyrannulus.c: Tyrannulus (ti-ran’a-lus), n. [NL. (Vieillot, 1816), dim. of Tyrannus, q.v.] A genus of very small tyrant-flycatchers of tropical America, of the subfamily Hlzniinz. The type is 7. ela- tus, the socalled gold-naped wren of early writers, about Tyrannulus latus. 22 inches long, with yellow crest, white throat, and short bill, tail, and wings, inhabiting the valley of the Amazon, and found northward to Panama.:

tyrannus.c: Tyrannus (ti-ran’us), ». [NL. (Cuvier, 1800), L. tyrannus, tyrant: see tyrant.]| The fame-giving genus of Tyrannide, formerly loosely extended to embrace most of the larger species then known (so named from their irritable or irascible disposition and their tendency to tyrannize over other birds), now restricted to a few large stout flycatchers like the common kingbird or bee-martin of the United States, T. tyrannus, T. pipiri, T. intrepidus, or T. caroli- mensis. They have the head with a vertical crest, the bill stout, hooked, and well-bristled, several outer primaries emarginate, the tail even or emarginate, and the coloration black and white, or gray and white, or olive and yellow. The gray kingbird of the West Indies and southern United States (7. dominicensis or T.. griseous), the Arkansas flycatcher (7. verticalis) of the Western States and Territories, Cassin’s and Couch’s flycatchers of the Southwestern States and southward (7. vociferant and 7’. melancholious), are additional examples; and others occur in the West Indies and Central and South America. See cut under kingbird.

tyranny.c: tyranny (tir’a-ni),.; pl. tyrannies (-nil). [¢ ME. tirannye, < OF. (and F.) tyrannic = Pr. ti- rannia = Sp. tiranta = Pg. tyrannic = It. tiran- nia, < ML. tyrannic, tyrania, < Gr. tupavvia, Tv- pavvic, tyranny, < tipavvoc, a tyrant: see tyrant.] 1. The rule of a tyrant in the ancient sense; the personal government of one of the Greek tyrants; a state or government having an uncontrolled ruler bearing the title of tyrant. His [Cypselus’s] moderation and clemency are allowed by all; yet he is universally called by the Grecian writers Tyrant of Corinth, and his government a Tyranny. J. Adams, Works, IV. 507. One might have thought... that, amid the endless changes that went on among the small commonwealths and tyrannies of that region, it would have been easier for the Republic to establish its dominion there than to establish it over great cities like Padua and Verona. E. A. Freeman, Venice, p. 288. 2. The office or incumbency of a tyrant; a tyrants administration or tenure; the system of government by tyrants. Aristotle... assigns to the tyranny of Periander a duration of 44 years. Smith’s Dict. Gr. and Rom. Biog., III. 191. Hence—8. A tyrannical government; a lawless autocracy or despotism. Polybius,... in the Sixth Book of his History, says thus: “When Princes began to indulge their own Lusts and sensual Appetites, then Kingdoms were turned into so many Tyrannies.” Milton, Answer to Salmasius, 4. Arbitrary or unrestrained exercise of power; despotic abuse of authority; unmerciful rule. Insulting tyranny begins to jet Upon the innocent and aweless throne. Shak., Rich. ITI., ii. 4. 51. The tyranny of wealthy and powerful subjects was the charactéristic evil of the times. Macaulay, Hallam’s Const. Hist. 5. A tyrannical action or proceeding; an instance of despotic rule or conduct. My meditations are how to revenge Thy bloody tyrannies. Lust’s Dominion, v. 2. Tis a tyranny Over an humble and obedient sweetness Ungently to insult. Ford, Lady’s Trial, v. 2. tyranny 6. Severity; harshness; stringency. The tyranny of the open night’s too rough For nature to endure. Shak., Lear, iii. 4. 2. =Syn. 1. Despotism, Autocracy, etc. See despotism.—4, Oppression, Despotism, etc. See oppression.

tyrant.c: tyrant (ti’rant), ». [Early mod. E. also tyrant, also tyran, tyranny; < ME. tyrant, tyrant, ty- aunt, traunt, also tyran, tiran, < OF. tyrant (with unorig -t), tiran, tyran, F. tyran = Pr. tran = Sp. titano = Pg. tyranny = It. tiranno = D. tiran, tyran = G. Sw. tyrant = Dan. tyran, < Li. tyrannus, < Gr. ripavvoc, lord, master, sovereign, tyrant; root unknown.] 1. In ancient Greece, an irresponsible chief or magistrate with unlimited powers, owing his office primarily to insurrection or usurpation. ‘The first tyrants, so called, were generally the leaders of risings against the oligarchies during the seventh and sixth centuries B. 0. They ruled with the popular consent in nearly all the Greek states and colonies at one time or another, transmitting their power to their heirs until democracies or new oligarchies overthrew them. Others raised themselves to the position by direct conquest or conspiracy. The arbitrary government of the tyrants was sometimes beneficent, but more often extremely oppressive and cruel. The typical tyrant in the latter sense of the word was Dionysius the Elder, of Syracuse (405 - 367 B. ©.). The tyrant of the Chersonese Was freedom’s best and bravest friend; That tyrant was Miltiades! Byron, Don Juan, iii. 86 (song). Hence —2. A wilfully arbitrary monarch or person in authority; a ruler or master who uses his power cruelly or oppressively; any person who treats those bound to him in any way as slaves to his will; an autocratic oppressor. Let us define a Tyrant, not according to vulgar conceits, but the judgment of Aristotle, and of all Learned Men. He is a Tyrant who regards his own welfare and profit only, and not that of the People. Milton, Ans. to‘Salmasius, xii. A tyrant cannot reign and oppress by his single force; he must really interest, and interest prodigiously, a sufficient number of subordinate tyrants in the duration of his power. Ames, Works, II. 280. 3. A tyrannical or compulsory influence; something that constrains the will inexorably; an overruling power. For lordly love is such a Tyranne fell That where he rules all power he doth expel. Spenser, Shep. Cal., October. Thought emancipated itself from expression without becoming its tyrant. Lowell, Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 326, 4. In ornith., a tyrant-flycatcher; one of the Tyrannide.—Bald tyrant. Same as baldhead, 3.— The Thirty Tyrants, a committee of thirty sympathizers with the oligarchs and with Sparta, who ruled Athens with absolute power 404-403 B. Cc. They were overthrown by the democracy under Thrasybulus. tyrant} (ti’rant),v. [Early mod. E. also tyran; < tyrant, n.) I. trans. To tyrannize over. What glorie or what guerdon hast thou [Love] found In feeble Ladies tyranning so sore? Spenser, ¥. Q., IV. vii. 1. II. intrans. To play the tyrant; tyrannize: sometimes with indefinite 7. This encouraged the Irish grandees (their O’s and Mac’s) to rant and tyrant it in their respective seignories. Fuller, Worthies, Buckinghamshire, I. 203.

tyrantchat.c: tyrant-chat (ti’rant-chat),. Some tyrant-fly- catcher which resembles or suggests a chat.

tyrantflycatcher.c: tyrant-flycatcher (ti’rant-fli’kach-ér),n. Aty- rant-bird; any member of the Tyrannide. tyrantlyt+ (ti’rant-li), adv. [< ME. tyrauntly; < tyrant + -ly?.) In the manner of a tyrant; tyrannically. He askyde me tyrauntly tribute of Rome, That tenefully tent was in time of mine elders. Morte Arthure (E. B. T. 8.), 1. 271.

tyrantryt.c: tyrantryt (ti’rant-ri), ». Same as tyranny. Wyclif, 3 Ki. (1 Ki.) xvi. 20.

tyrantshrike.c: tyrant-shrike (ti’rant-shrik), ». One of the larger tyrant-flycatchers with a stout bill resembling a shrike’s, as any species of the genus Tyrannus proper, like the kingbird or bee-martin. Some of these used to be placed in the genus Lanius, being mistaken for shrikes. See cut under kingbird.

tyrantwren.c: tyrant-wren (ti’rant-ren),. One of the smaller tyrant-flyeatchers, as a species of Tyrannulus, resembling a wren in some respects. See cut under Tyrannulus. tyre}, An obsolete spelling of tire. 6566 tyre? (sir), ». [E.Ind.] A preparation of milk and rice used by the East Indians.

tyras.c: Tyras (tl'ras). The ancient name of the river Dniester.

tyre.c: Tyre (sir). [L.Tyrus,Gv. T vog, from Phen. (Heb.) Tsor (gor, modern our), rock.] Next to Sidon, the oldest and most important city of Phenicia. It consisted of a town on the mainland, which was the oldest part (Palsetyrus), and two rocky islands directly opposite Palsetyrus. These islands originally contained only the temple of Melkarth and warehouses. In the 13th century B. C. they were more settled, and they were united by Hiram, the contemporary of Solomon, by an embank¬ ment. In the 11th century B. C. Tyre began, under its first king, Abibaal, father of Hiram, to rival its mother city Sidon, and soon supplanted it as queen of the Phenician cities. Of its magnificence and luxury the prophet Ezekiel gives a detailed and graphic description. It established colo¬ nies in Sicily, Sardinia, Spain, Africa (Carthage), and sent out mercantile fleets to India and Brittany. Under Hiram Tyre reached the height of its prosperity and splendor. It then cameinto close friendly relations with Israel. Later, Ahab, king of Israel, married Jezebel, daughter of Eth- baal, whose greatgranddaughter Elissa (Dido) is said to have founded Carthage. Tyre was often the aim of at¬ tacks by Eastern rulers. It became tributary to Assyria under Tiglath-Pileser III. (745-727 B. C.). Shalmaneser IV. (727-722) besieged it for five years, apparently without success. Under Nebuchadnezzar it stood a siege of 13

tyremesis.c: tyremesis (ti-rem’e-sis), n. [< Gr. rupdc, cheese, + éueowc, vomiting: see emesis.] Vomiting of cheesy or curdy matters. Also tyrosis.

tyrian.c: Tyrian (tir’i-an),a@.andn. [= F. Tyrien, < L. Tyrius, < Gr. Tipioc, < Tipoc, L. Tyrus, Tyre (see def.).] I. a. 1. Of or pertaining to the ancient city and state of Tyre in Phenicia, on the Mediterranean.— 2, Of a purple color characteristic of Tyre.— Tyrian Cynosure, the constellation Ursa Minor, anciently called the Cynosure, which served as a guide to the Tyrians in their long voyages. And thou shalt be our star of Arcady, Or Tyrian cynosure. Milton, Comus, 1. 342. Tyrian purple. See purple. IT, ». A native of Tyre.

tyriasis.c: tyriasis (ti-ri’a-sis), n. [« Gr. tupdc, cheese, + -basis.] 1. Elephantiasis Arabum.—2. Falling off of the hair; alopecia.

tyro.c: tyro (ti’ro), n. [Formerly, and prop., tiro; <L. tiro, misspelled tyro, a newly levied soldier, a young soldier.] A beginner in learning anything; one who is employed in learning or who has mastered the rudiments only of any branch of knowledge; a novice. There stands a structure on a rising hill, Where tyros take their freedom out to kill. Garth, Dispensary, iii. tirocinium} (ti-ro-sin’i-um), ». Same as tyrociny. Gayton. Compare tirocinium.

tyrociny.c: tyrociny (ti-ros’i-ni), ». [Prop. *tyrociny; < L. tirocinium, first service or trial, < tivo, a newly levied soldier: see tyro.] The state of being a tyro, beginner, or learner; pupilage; apprenticeship ; unskilled effort. To thee I write my Apotheosie, Meecenas, strengthen my Tyrocinie. Tourneur, Yrans. Metamorphosis, Ded.

tyroglyphide.c: Tyroglyphide (ti-ro-glif/i-dé), n. pl. [NL., < Tyroglyphus + -idz.] A family of atracheate Acarina, typified by the genus Tyrogiyphus. They all have eight legs developed, of five joints apiece, chelate mandibles, skeleton composed of sclerites in a soft skin, and two front pairs of legs set below the body. The Tyroglyphidz are usually parasitic during the curious hypopial stage, although they do not seem to require any nutriment from the host; and somespecies would appear to be parasitic in the adult stage, as Glyciphagus balena- rum. The related families Sarcoptide and Myobiide are strictly parasitic during every stage of their existence.

tyroglyphus.c: Tyroglyphus (ti-rog’li-fus), ». [NL. (La- treille, 1796), < Gr. tupek, cheese, + yAider, carve.] A notable genus of acarids or mites, typical of the family Tyroglyphidz, having a tarsal claw and a sucker. Those of the subgenus Rhizoglyphus feed upon vegetable products, and comprise Phylloxera-mite (Tyvoglyphus phylloxera). a, dorsal view of female; 4, ventral view of female; c, mouthparts; d, /,g,,forms of tarsal appendages; e, ventral tubercles of male. (All the figures are much enlarged.) about a dozen species. Those of Tyroglyphus proper feed upon animal. products, and include among others the wellknown cheese-mites, 7. sivo and 7. longior—the latter feeding also upon farinaceous substances. (See cut under Jlour-mite.) T. phylloxera preys upon the grapevine phylloxera; 7’. entomophagous is a wellknown pest in entomological collections.

tyroler.c: Tyroler (ti-ro’ler), n. [« G. Tyroler, Tiroler, a Tyrolese, < Tyrol, Tirol, Tyrol: see Tyrolese.] A native of Tyrol; a Tyrolese. [Rare.]

tyrolese.c: Tyrolese (tir-0-lés’ or -léz’), a. and n. [< Tyrol (G. Tirol, and improperly Tyrol) + -ese.] I. a. Of or pertaining to Tyrol (often called the Tyrol), an Alpine province forming with Vor- arlberg a crownland of the Cisleithan division of Austria-Hungary. II. n. sing. and pl. A native or the natives tzopilotl (ts0’ pi-lotl), n. of Tyrol. tzopilotl

tyrolienne.c: Tyrolienne (ti-r6-li-en’), n. [I., fem. of Tyro- lien, of or pertaining to Tyrol, ¢ Tyrol, Tyrol.) A dance of the Tyrolese peasants, or a song or melody suitable for such a dance. The characteristic folksongs of Tyrol abound in yodels.

tyroline.c: tyroline (tir’6-lin), ». <A violet dye produced by treatment of aniline; aniline violet. Ure, Dict., IT. 1050.

tyrolite.c: tyrolite (tir’6-lit), ». [Also tyrolite; < Tyrol + -ite2.] A hydrous arseniate of copper, occurring in orthorhombic crystals and in aggregates having a foliated micaceous structure. It is very soft, sectile, and flexible in thin scales, and has a bluish-green color. It is known from a number of localities, but is named from that at Falkenstein in Tyrol.

tyroma.c: tyroma (ti-ro’mii),n. [NL., < Gr. trupéc, cheese.] Falling off of the hair; alopecia.

tyrone.c: Tyrone (ti-ron'). A county in Ulster, Ireland, bounded by Donegal, Londonderry, Lough Neagh, Armagh, Monaghan, and Fermanagh. Capital, Omagh. The surface is generally hilly. Area, 1,260 square miles. Population (1891), 171,278. Tyrone, Earl of. See O’Neil, Hugh.

tyronism.c: tyronism (ti’r6-nizm), n. [< tyro(n-) + -ism.] The state of being a tyro. Also tironism.

tyropoeoil.c: Tyropoeoil (tir-o-pe'on). [Gr. tu TvpoTTot&v, of the cheese-makers.] A valley at Jerusalem. See the extract. The Pool of Siloam lies on the opposite side of this ridge, at the mouth of the valley called that of the Cheesemak- ers (Tyropoeon) in the time of Josephus, but which is now filled up with rubbish, and in large part built over. Sayce, Anc. Monuments, p. 98.

tyrosin.c: tyrosin (ti’rd-sin), n. [Ivreg. < Gr. ripoc, cheese, + -in2.] A white crystalline body, odorless, and insoluble in cold water, having the formula CoHy,NO3. It is an amido-acid, and forms salts with both acids and bases. It is a product of the decomposition of proteids, either by the ferment trypsin, by putrefaction, or by boiling with acids.

tyrosis.c: tyrosis (ti-ro’sis),. [NL.,< Gr. rupdc, cheese, + -osis.] 1. Same as tyremesis.— 2. The curdling of milk.

tyrothrix.c: tyrothrix (ti’rd-thriks), m. [INL., < Gr. rupee, cheese, + Opié, hair.] A bacterium found in cheese.

tyrotoxicon.c: tyrotoxicon (ti-r6-tok’si-kon), m. [NL., ¢ Gr. tupobc, cheese, + roguxdv, poison.] A ptomaine produced in milk or cheese, the cause of the symptoms of poisoning occasionally observed to follow the eating of ice-cream. It is either identical with or closely related to diazobenzol. Tyrrel’s case. See casel. Tyrrel’s fascia. The rectovesical fascia. Tyrrel’s hook, A fine hook used in certain operations on the eye for drawing forward the iris.

tyrrhene.c: Tyrrhene (ti-rén’), a. [<L. Tyrrhenus,< Gr. Tup- pyvoc, < Tuppyvia, the Gr. name of Etruria or Tuscany.] Same as Tyrrhenian.

tyrrhenian.c: Tyrrhenian (ti-ré’ni-an), a.andn. [< Tyrrhene + -ian.] I, a. Etruscan: used poetically, or in connection with subjects having some Greek relation or bearing.—Tyrrhenian Sea, a name still used for that part of the Mediterranean which lies between Tuscany and the mainland southward and the islands of Sardinia and Corsica. II. ». An Etruscan. tyrritt, 7. An old spelling of térret.

tyrrhenians.c: Tyrrhenians (ti-re'ni-anz). A name given by the Greeks to the ancient inhabitants of Etruria. Tyrrhenian Sea, or Inferum Mare (in'f e-rum raa're). In ancient geography, that part of the Mediterranean which lies west of Italy.

tyrtseus.c: Tyrtseus (ter-te'us). [Gr. Tup-raiof.] Lived in 1017 the middle of the 7th century B. c. A famous elegiac poet of Sparta, said to have been a native of Attica. According to a (doubtless un¬ founded) tradition, the Spartans who were at war with the Messenians were commanded by the oracle to take a leader from among the Athenians. The latter, not wish¬ ing to aid tile Spartans, sent Tyrtseus, a lame schoolmaster of no reputation; but by his songs he so inspired his fol¬ lowers that they obtained the victory. Fragments of his poems are extant. Cyrus (ti'rus). The Latin name of Tyre.

tyrtzan.c: Tyrtzan (tér-té’an), a. [< L. Tyrteus, < Gr. Tupraioc, Tyrteeus (see def.), + -an.] Of or pertaining to Tyrteus, a Greek poet of the seventh century B.C., who wrote marching-songs and elegiac exhortations for the Spartans. tyrant, ”. A variant of tisane.

tyrwhitt.c: Tyrwhitt (ter'it), Thomas. Born at London, March 29, 1730: died at London, Aug. 15, 1786. An English critic. He studied at Oxford, and was elected a fellow of Merton in 1755, but in 1762 abandoned his academic career in order to become clerk of the House of Commons. He resigned his clerkship in 1768, and de¬ voted himself to literature. He wrote “ Observations on Some Passages of Shakespeare ” (1766), and prepared excellent editions of Chaucer’s “ Canterbury Tales ” (1775-78) and Aristotle’s “ Poetics ” (1794). He is chiefly known as the original editor of “ Rowley’s Poems,” which he demon¬ stated were written by Chatterton.

tyrwhittthomas.c: Tyrwhitt, Thomas (1730-1786). English antiquary (editor of Chaucer). Tyrwhitt Tytler, Sarah. See Keddie. Udall, John (died 1592). English nonconformist divine. J. Udall

tysonian.c: Tysonian (ti-s0’ni-an), a. [< Tyson (see def.) + -ian.] Of or pertaining to, or named after, the anatomist Tyson: specifying the preputial glands or follicles which secrete the sebaceous substance smegma.

tysonite.c: tysonite (ti’son-it), ~. [After 8. T. Tyson, the discoverer.] A rare fluorid of the cerium metals, occurring in hexagonal crystals and massive, of a wax-yellow color: found in Colorado. Tyson’s glands. See gland and Tysonian. tyssewt, 7. An old spelling of tissue.

tystie.c: tystie (tis’ti), ». The black guillemot, Uria grylle. See cut under guillemot. [Orkney and Shetland.] tytt, tytet, tyttet, adv. Obsolete spellings of title, tythet,”.andv. An obsolete spelling of tithes. tything, 7. An obsolete spelling of tithing. tythingst, ». An obsolete form of tidings. See tiding. Tyzack’s anchor. tzar, tzarina, etc. See czar, etc. tzetze, tzetse, ». See tsetse.

tyt.c: tyt, v. An old spelling of tiel. -ty!. [< ME. -ty, -ti, < AS. -tig, etc., a suffix, in Goth. a separate noun, ‘a ten’ or ‘decade,’ = Goth. titus; a form of ten, used in numerals: see ten, and the words twenty, etc., as cited.] A termination of numerals—namely, in twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty,»seventy, eighty, ninety, originally meaning ‘ten’ (twenty, ‘twain tens,’ thirty, ‘three tens,’ etc.). -ty?. [< ME. -tie, -tye, -tee, -te, < OF. -te, -tee, F. -té = Sp. -dad = Pg. -dade = It. -td, -tate, -tade, < L. -tas (-tat-), usually preceded by a stem-vowel -7- (-its, > E. -ity), a suffix used to form abstract nouns from adjectives, as in agilitas, agility, < agilis, agile, bonitas, goodness, < bonus, good, units, oneness, < nus, one, etc.] A suffix appearing in many abstract nouns taken or formed from the Latin, as in agility, anxiety, benignity, humanity, unity, etc. It is commonly preceded, as in these cases, by a stem-vowel -7- (the termination -ity being so common as to be often used as an English formative); but in some words the original vowel has disappeared, as in bounty, loyalty, royalty, etc., or none existed in the Latin, as in liberty, poverty, etc. In some words the suffix is not recognized as such, as in city. tyall, ». [Perhaps irreg. ¢ tiel, formerly tye, + -al (?).] A bell-rope, or something tied toa bell for ringing it. The great bell’s clapper was fallen down, the tyall was broken, so that the bishop could not be rung into the town. Latimer, 6th Serm. bef. Edw. VI., 1549. Tyburn ticket. A certificate formerly given to the prosecutor of a felon to conviction, the original proprietor or first assignee of it being exempted by a statute of William III. from all parish and ward offices within the parish or ward where the felony had been committed. Two-way Cock. a, position which distributes water to two branches; 6, c, positions in which the water is pases through only one branch; d, position for stopping flow. Tyburn tippet Tyburn tippett. See tippet. Tyburn tree. See tree.

tytler.c: Tytler (tlt'ler), Alexander Fraser, Lord Woodhouselee. Born at Edinburgh, Oct. 15, 1747: died there, Jan. 5, 1813. A Scottish historical and general writer, son of William Tytler (judgeadvocate of Scotland). Among his works are “ Elements of General History ” (1801: first published as “ Outlines ” 1782), lives of Lord Karnes (1807)and of Petrarch (1810), “ Essay on the Principles of Translation ” (1791). Tytler, C. C. Fraser. The pseudonym of Mrs. Christina Catherine Fraser Tytler Liddell. Tytler, Patrick Fraser. Born at Edinburgh, Aug. 30, 1791: died at Great Malvern, England, Dec. 24, 1849. A Scottish historian, son of A. Tzum6 F. Tytler. Jlis chief work is a “History of Scotland” (9 vols. 1828-43). Among his other works are lives of Admirable Crichton, Wyclif, Raleigh, and Henry VIII. “Lives of Scottish Worthies " (1831-33), and “Progress of Discovery on the Northern Coasts of America ’’ (1832). Tytler, Sarah. The pseudonym of Henrietta Keddie. Tytler, William. Born at Edinburgh, Oct. 12, 1711: died at Edinburgh, Sept. 12. 1792. A Scottish historical and antiquarian writer. His chief work is “ An Inquiry, Historical and Critical, into the Evidence against Mary Queen of Scots ” (1760).

tyumenortiumen.c: Tyumen, or Tiumen (tyo-meny'). A town in the government of Tobolsk, West Siberia, situ¬ ated on the Tura about 140 miles southwest of Tobolsk. It has important commerce through the Obi river-system; is the terminus of a railway from Yekaterinburg; and is on the great Siberian highway. It is the chief manufacturing center in Siberia: among its manufactures are leather and carpets. Tz. For Kussian words in Tz, see Ts.

tzanaortsana.c: Tzana, or Tsana (tsa'na),orDembea (dem'ba- a), Lake. A lake in the interior of Abyssinia, intersected by lat. 12° N. Its outlet is the Blue Nile. Elevation above sealevel, about 5,700 feet. Length, 55 miles.

tzigane.c: Tzigane (tse-gan'), La. An opera by Strauss, produced at Paris in 1877.

tzigany.c: Tzigany (tsig’a-ni), ». and a. [Hung. Cigany, Tagany (cf. It. Zingano, Zingaro, G. Zigeuner, etc.), Gipsy: see under Gipsy.] I, n. A Hungarian Gipsy. II, a. Of or pertaining to Hungarian Gipsies: used in English chiefly with reference to their music. See anchor, 1. (Mex.] Same as zopilote. We SEASON Satay 1. The twenty-first character and fifth vowel-sign in the English alphabet. The Phenician alphabet, from which ours comes ultimately (see under A), had no such sign, but ended with 7. A sign for the unsound (that is, for 90, or 6, as it is represented in the respelling of this dictionary) was added by the Greeks when they adapted the Phenician signs to their own use, and was written indifferently V or Y; but the latter finally established itself as the accepted form in Greek usage, while the former became customary in the derived Italian alphabets; so that, considerably later, the Romans were able to import Y as a separate and foreign character, to represent the foreign Greek sound v% (= French u, German%i or ue), into which the Greek 6 had meanwhile become to a great extent altered in pronunciation. The V was also commonly written with its angle rounded, as U; and V and U were for a long time merely different forms of the same sign (like Jand J): itis only recently that they have come to be always distinctly held apart, and have different values given them. As W also is a doubled U or JV, it appears that our four letters U, V, W, and Y all come from single sign added by the Greeks at the end of the Phenician system. The sound originally and properly represented by the character, and still belonging to it in most languages outside of English, is the 00 or 6 sound, as in mood, move, rule, and the like, the closest of the labial vowels, or rounded vowels, as they are often called (see under O); but this value the letter has in English only in exceptional cases. What we call ‘‘long wu,” namely, is this same sound with the semivowel y prefixed, as you (yo); and what we call ‘‘short uw” is the more open of the two shades of neutral vowel-sound. The digraphs we, eu, and ew also have, as long, the yé-value in the same manner and degree. The y-element in the sound, namely, is not always alike full and undeniable, but varies somewhat, according to the difficulty of slipping it in after a preceding consonant. The difficulty in the way of inserting the y, however, is removed if the preceding syllable has the accent; and hence even those who pronounce pend'rious say pen’wry, and so in all other like cases. This omission of the y-element is not approved, but is stigmatized as provincial or vulgar, although practised by many educated and careful speakers, and probably becoming more prevalent.
